source.title: Conformer-1: Robust ASR via Large-Scale Semisupervised Bootstrapping
source.authors: Kevin Zhang; Luka Chkhetiani; Francis McCann Ramirez; Yash Khare; Andrea Vanzo; Michael Liang; Sergio Ramirez Martin; Gabriel Oexle; Ruben Bousbib; Taufiquzzaman Peyash; Mike Nguyen; Dillon Pulliam; Domenic Donato

record.tranche_reason: The study uses a scaling-law heuristic to choose a speech-data quantity, then reports ASR performance from adding pseudo-labeled data. It does not test the claimed loss power laws or fit them.
record.gate_note: The study cites scaling laws and adapts a tokens-per-parameter ratio to estimate an optimal number of speech-data hours. Its results are WER and proper-noun metrics, not held-out cross-entropy loss or fitted power-law behavior. It does not test prediction from small runs, architecture-shape effects, downstream predictability from pretraining loss, or the scaling-law fitting choices in V7.
record.test_reason: The study uses the Chinchilla ~20 tokens-per-parameter ratio (Hoffmann et al., Table A3) to set a speech-data budget of about 550k hours for a 264M-parameter ASR model (Appendix C). It then reports WER and proper-noun gains from adding pseudo-labeled data at fixed model size. It fits no power law and reports no held-out loss curves. It runs no extrapolation, compute-optimal sweep, shape ablation or loss-to-downstream mapping. The 550k-hour figure is an input to its training design, not a tested prediction.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that adding pseudo-labeled public speech data cuts relative WER by 11.5% (async) and 24.3% (realtime) and improves noise robustness. They also say this lets them train state-of-the-art ASR without large human-labeled data. They describe the 550k-hour target as derived by adapting the Hoffmann et al. ratio, and claim that data-only scaling 'in accordance with the scaling laws' gives sizeable gains. That claim is not tested against alternatives.
record.recipe_differences: They adapt a tokens-per-parameter heuristic to estimate speech-data hours and vary data quantity for fixed-size ASR models; they report WER and proper-noun metrics rather than fitting held-out language-model loss curves.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper says data saturation depends on model type and pseudo-label quality: the async model's additional-data benefit tapers after 100k hours, while the realtime model continues to benefit beyond 250k hours. It attributes part of the difference to the quality gap between the pseudo-label-generating model and each baseline.

fits_no_version.finding: For the async model (264M), Table 2 average WER goes 8.7, 8.3, 7.9, 7.7, 7.6, 7.7 as pseudo-labeled data rises from 0 to 520k hours. The gain largely saturates by about 120k hours, well below the 550k hours from the adapted Chinchilla ratio.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this ASR setup, WER gains from extra pseudo-labeled data at fixed model size saturate well before the data size implied by a text-derived tokens-per-parameter ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: The smaller realtime model (130M) keeps gaining past 250k hours while the larger async model tapers after 100k. The authors say this 'seems to contradict' larger models having higher saturation points. They attribute it to the pseudo-labels coming from the async baseline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: With self-generated pseudo-labels, the data saturation point depends on the gap between label quality and model quality, not only on model size.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding pseudo-labeled data improves proper-noun Jaro-Winkler distance by 7.6% relative for the async model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In this ASR setup, pseudo-labeled data can improve proper-noun transcription metrics.

record.problems: The scaling-law connection is based on an adapted heuristic, not a fit or test of power-law curves. Outcomes are ASR metrics rather than held-out cross-entropy loss; the reported text does not provide uncertainty estimates for the scaling results.
record.rows_left_out: The paper gives domain-level results for multiple pseudo-labeled data quantities in Tables 2 and 3, but their flattened text extraction makes individual metric-to-condition assignments ambiguous. The aggregate relative improvements stated explicitly in Section 3.1 are recorded instead.

untested.parts: Whether a power-law form holds for data scaling in speech recognition. Only 5–6 data points of WER at fixed model size are reported, with no fit and no loss measure.
The tokens-per-parameter ratio is transferred to speech through assumed words-per-minute and tokens-per-word constants. Its optimality for speech is never checked against other data or model sizes.

record.verdict_notes: The paper cites Hoffmann et al. (ref [2]) for 'power scaling laws' and for under-trained LLMs. In Appendix C, 'TPW 43' is likely a flattened 4/3. That reading reproduces 550k hours: 264M×20/(120×4/3×60). The 0.5 WER-point differences between data sizes have no uncertainty estimates. The noise-robustness results (Figure 5) are a different construct and bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: The study scales pseudo-labeled speech data and reports ASR metrics, but does not test whether a power-law form holds in speech.

rows.subject: Async model
rows.operation_detail: Trained with varying quantities of pseudo-labeled data added to 57k hours of labeled data.
rows.baseline: Model trained on 57k hours of labeled data only
rows.note: The paper reports this aggregate improvement in prose; it is WER, not cross-entropy loss or a fitted power law.

rows.note: The paper describes this as a relative accuracy improvement and discusses it in the context of WER; it is not cross-entropy loss or a fitted power law.
rows.check: The condition says 500k hours, following the prose. Table 3's largest row is 'A + 520k pseudo', and its average WER of 11.9 to 9.0 (about 24.4% relative) matches the stated 24.3%. The condition should read 520k, with a note that the prose says 500k. The measure is relative average WER reduction, which the paper calls 'accuracy improvement'.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
